title: Hazel Restaurant Is Back in Occidental — And More Hazel Than Ever
summary:
The pot roast is braising, the vegan Caesar is back and the schnitzel hangs off the plate. Hazel has reopened in Occidental in a quirky old Victorian that may fit the beloved restaurant better than ever.

The post Hazel Restaurant Is Back in Occidental — And More Hazel Than Ever appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sometimes when a door closes, a 150-year-old yellow clapboard Victorian overlooking downtown Occidental opens.

That’s exactly what happened to Jim and Michele Wimborough of Hazel Restaurant.

This week, the couple reopened Hazel in a new home at 3688 Bohemian Highway, less than a year after closing the restaurant’s longtime location down the street. That space, at 3782 Bohemian Highway, is now home to the recently opened Bohemian Bistro.

Moving wasn’t the plan. But sometimes unexpected changes come with silver linings.

The quirky old building that once housed Barley & Hops has a historic bar filled with 19th-century charm, an airy dining room, cozy nooks for tables and just the right amount of west county character to make it feel like a neighborhood restaurant from the start.

Not surprisingly, the regulars have already begun returning, Michele Wimborough said, happy to see their favorite dishes back on the menu.

A new home

The couple spent the past eight months reworking the space, which had sat empty for several years. It wasn’t a quick turnaround, or at least not as quick as anyone would have liked. Old buildings and old equipment have a way of revealing surprises, and sometimes things simply take longer than expected. That, too, is part of being a restaurateur.

On Aug. 13, with the tables set, cookies baked, pot roast braising and sourdough starter rising, Hazel soft-opened in its new home.

Naturally, one of the fryers broke. The sourdough starter balked. That’s also part of being a restaurateur.

Otherwise, Hazel might be more Hazel than ever.

Looking out onto a redwood grove from the pale blue dining room, there’s a coziness that settles over the room. A soft banquette, old wood floors, the occasional creak and tiny decorative details that reward a closer look all fit naturally with the casual comfort food that has become Hazel’s hallmark.

The limited opening menu includes the favorites: the epic hunk of braised beef with mashed potatoes, roasted half chicken, vegan Caesar salad and the OMG Sundae with caramel and hot fudge.

The schnitzel is larger than its oversized plate, its crisp coating spilling over the edges alongside red cabbage. The Brussels sprouts with bacon may be the best you’ve ever had, with crisp leaves, tender centers and just enough caramelization.

New are flatbreads topped with Point Reyes blue cheese, caramelized onions and bacon. They’re every bit as satisfying as Hazel’s old pizzas.

It’s all there, just the same, but in a new place that feels unmistakably Hazel.

Open 5-9 p.m. Wednesday through Monday. 3688 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-6003, restauranthazel.com.

title: Westerbeke Ranch in Sonoma Doubles as a Family’s Multigenerational Homestead
summary:
A family homestead for five generations, Sonoma’s Westerbeke Ranch has hosted notable visionaries in its storied evolution from family home to retreat and conference center.

The post Westerbeke Ranch in Sonoma Doubles as a Family’s Multigenerational Homestead appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Legend has it, there are “voices” in The Valley of the Moon. The Miwok and Pomo heard them as spirits or ghosts, visible in the illusion of multiple moons, a legend retold by author Jack London in his 1913 novel of the same name. Contemporary listeners cite the voices as echoes of nature.

In either case, if voices do whisper through this valley of rolling hills, wildflowers, and scattered oaks, Sonoma’s Westerbeke Ranch would be the place to hear them. A family homestead for five generations, its wooden beams and adobe walls were drawn from the surrounding earth more than 80 years ago. In its storied evolution from family home to retreat and conference center, it has hosted notable visionaries such as Joseph Campbell, Stan Grof, Werner Erhard, and Elisabeth Kübler-Ross.

With its smooth archways, weathered beams, and ceramic-tiled roofs, the ranch feels like an authentic early Californian hacienda. Comfortable gathering spaces surround a central patio and a pool. Well-tended, but unfussy gardens wrap around pathways that lead through dappled shade to the property’s guest cabins. From furnishings and artifacts to artwork and plantings, everything has been curated to flow in harmony with the natural surroundings.

The 11-acre property on Grove Street is overseen by owner and CEO Wendy Westerbeke, who still makes her home here. She credits the rustic ambience and authenticity of the place to her grandparents, Muriel and “Dick” Van Hoosear, who purchased and built on the property in the 1930s.

Grandfather Van Hoosear, she says, was an adventurous and peripatetic builder, raised in the East Bay, who bounced between California and favorite places like Mexico, Arizona, and the Four Corners region, where he gathered inspiration, artifacts, and salvaged materials like old hardware, hinges, and tile.

The timeworn timbers of the ceiling beams, window frames, and heavy doors reveal the ridges of old-growth wood he rescued locally from aging fences and crumbling barns. “He always had a project,” Westerbeke recalls. “He would come here on weekends, jump out of his car, leave the door open, run to the tool room to do things on the property. There was a lot going on at once.”

The property’s central dining room showcases Van Hoosear’s talents. The adobe walls, now painted a warm white, were made with mud from the bottom of a former reservoir on the property. His handmade fireplace still serves as a focal point, a rustic-yet-majestic construction of local stones that occupies a charming alcove they call “the walk-in.”

A walled courtyard attached to the dining room features Spanish-style rustic brick and tilework, with arched nichos framing plants and artifacts. “This kind of patina—you can’t create this stuff,” Westerbeke says, running her hand over the deeply ridged grain of a door. “There’s so much imitation around now, but this is the real deal.”

The term “real deal” could also be applied to “Grandpa Dick” himself, who appears in black-and-white photos throughout the property, along with dozens of other historical family photos. In one, he appears with wife Muriel, wearing worn chaps and Southwestern accessories, in the Tom Mix-style cowboy chic popular in early 20th-century America.

In 1936, her grandparents put in the 40-by-70-foot pool that guests use to this day. The couple raised their three daughters there, one of whom was Westerbeke’s mother, Patricia.

In the 1960s, Patricia and her husband Donald Westerbeke began hosting yoga retreats and meditations at the ranch, riding the wave of interest in alternative healing and Eastern medicine. As word-of-mouth traveled through the psychology corridors of UC Berkeley and spiritual centers such as the Esalen Institute, a who’s-who of humanist psychologists and New Age thinkers flocked to the property for community and inspiration.

When Donald suffered a pituitary gland tumor, it was an alternative healer that suggested he explore alternative therapies. He recovered, and Westerbeke’s parents became devoted to the idea that well-being is tied to state of mind, and that changing personal attitudes can actually improve health. Westerbeke herself studied psychology specializing in art therapy and, in her 20s, returned home with a vision to help her parents grow and manage the business.

Today the property holds five charming cabins that sleep up to 48 people. With the gardens, the large dining room, and sprawling pool, it makes a popular package for weddings and family reunions.

Additionally, conference spaces offer four distinctive meeting rooms that can handle groups from 15-80 people. Westerbeke estimates 80% of her conference and retreat clientele are women—often healthcare workers, psychologists, and educators—people, she acknowledges, “who really need a break.” Others are companies seeking unity, or a fresh start. They have several repeat customers that talk about lasting bonds forged from experiences there, delightful farm-to-table meals, and memorable gatherings.

“Because it’s peaceful and has this kind of energy, remarkable things do happen here,” Westerbeke says. “I think that’s what my parents really wanted, and that’s what I want to pass down, is that this can be a respite from the world.”

On a recent weekday morning, a group of 20 or so people studying to be personal coaches sat in a circle, attention rapt on their speaker, while a colorful luncheon of fresh salads and chicken sliders awaited in the main dining room. Later they laughed and shared stories outdoors on an adjoining sunny patio overlooking the pool and grounds.

“I think one of my favorite things about this place is people’s responses to being here,” Westerbeke says. “We have guest books going back… and it’s all these people writing about how they change their lives here. They come to workshops, and they recognize something about their patterns, and they become a completely different person because of their visit here. We’re just really the vessel for this to happen in.”

Recent additions to the property include an updated residence for Westerbeke and her husband, Ted Bucklin, after the couple decided to offer the family’s main house to her daughter’s family to live in. In her new home, Westerbeke’s vivid floral paintings adorn the walls, evoking the colorful gardens of the property itself and the 163-acre Van Hoosear Wildflower Preserve across the road, which the family still owns but has set up as an open space conservation easement managed by the Sonoma Ecology Center. The lower level serves as her painting studio, complete with her own stunning landscapes, and a special area for her to “paint with the grandchildren.”

Another new addition is a tall, narrow hay-bale structure with a weathered bell and chimes that echo within its second story, creating a sound bath below. A verse from Leonard Cohen’s “Anthem” is printed on the wall:

Ring the bells that still can ring, forget your perfect offering.

There is a crack in everything. That’s how the light gets in.

The structure looks like it has been there as long as the ranch itself, a testament to the care the family puts into maintaining harmony with the property’s original design.

“A lot of our colleagues and friends are wine- and grape-oriented,” Westerbeke reflects, “And, you know, I always joke, ‘Well, we don’t grow grapes here; we grow people.’ And it’s true. You know, people come here and it’s their spirits that get touched. And it’s a different kind of nurturing, but I love that.”

Learn more about Westerbeke Ranch at thewesterbekeranch.com. Wendy Westerbeke’s art can be found at wendywesterbekeart.com.

title: Lo & Behold Bar and Kitchen Is Healdsburg’s Favorite After Work Hangout
summary:
This late-night Healdsburg spot is dark and moody, but in a cozy-nest way, not a sticky-table-and-some-guy-passed-out-at-the-bar way.

The post Lo & Behold Bar and Kitchen Is Healdsburg’s Favorite After Work Hangout appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Healdsburg has no shortage of places to drink serious wine. Lo & Behold is where you go when you’re done being serious about it and just want a good cocktail.

The downtown bar has become a magnet for locals looking for a break from “Beverly Healdsburg,” but it is a particular favorite of the hospitality industry: restaurant workers, winemakers, tasting-room staff and others finally off the clock. That is exactly what Tara Heffernon and her business partners, Sean Kelley and Laura Sanfilippo, longtime industry veterans themselves, thought the increasingly touristy town needed.

“It’s the place you’re always looking for when you’re traveling,” Heffernon said — that laid-back insider’s spot where the locals actually eat and drink. “The biggest compliment we get is that people are being sent to us from another establishment.”

Inside the cavernous dining room are comfy chairs and a sofa for lingering, high-top tables, a long banquette lined with bistro tables and plenty of seats at the bar. It’s dark and moody, but in a cozy-nest way, not a sticky-table-and-some-guy-passed-out-at-the-bar way.

Outside, the casual patio is dog- and kid-friendly, with no one fretting over a few crumbs or what you’re wearing.

Heffernon still makes the signature sangria herself, filling it with whatever fruit and herbs are in season. Right now, that means black plums and shiso. It’s an unassuming cocktail that goes down easily after a long day of wine tasting. There’s no need to discuss its legs or finish because, really, who cares? It’s just fun to drink.

Lo & Behold is also one of the few spots in Healdsburg open after 9 p.m., something Heffernon and Sanfilippo knew from experience was sorely lacking in the sleepy town.

The backstory

Heffernon and Sanfilippo were part of the founding team at Duke’s Spirited Cocktails with Cappy Sorentino and Steven Maduro in 2016. The bar became known for working backyard botanicals into its drinks, creating fresh and unusual flavors that helped fuel the craft-cocktail wave that is now almost commonplace.

The team departed in 2021. Heffernon and Sanfilippo then teamed up with chef Kelley, who had run the food program at Burdock, to open Lo & Behold.

“We had an opportunity to start our own place and we wanted to create something really special together,” Heffernon said.

Sensing something was missing from Healdsburg — a warm, friendly, casual spot with good service — they plunged into creating Lo & Behold. Nearly five years later, the place is rarely empty.

“It’s just abuzz all of the time,” Heffernon said. “We want it to feel like people are coming home.”

Fun fact

Inside the men’s room (sorry, ladies), look for the clown painting by longtime comedian Red Skelton. You’ll see it, and it may haunt your nightmares.

When Guy Fieri is filming “Tournament of Champions” or “Guy’s Grocery Games,” celebrity chefs often stop by Lo & Behold for dinner and sign the print.

How long in business

Four years — five in January, according to Heffernon. She is already sweating the grand celebration they’ll throw because, she said, it has to be epic.

Most popular dish

The Almost Famous Chicken Tenders, because they’re the kind of adult kid food that makes people feel comforted and nurtured. But the soul of the menu, Heffernon said, is the Kimchi Noodles, made with broad, housemade noodles bathed in kimchi butter and black vinegar and topped with a generous dollop of kimchi.

When it comes to cocktails, the Guava Paloma has always been at the top of the list. A juicy twist on the Mexican highball, it’s made with white tequila, guava, grapefruit, lime and lychee — a little sweet, a little sour and dangerously delicious.

The food

Chef Kelley is a chef’s chef, meaning he makes the kind of food other chefs crave. He’s not interested in culinary bravado. Instead, he puts his efforts into hearty, rib-sticking, “I’m starving, feed me” food. His creative takes on global cuisine almost always hit the mark, with bold flavors and unusual — sometimes plain wacky — combinations that just work.

Tallow-braised radishes with beef floss ($13) are a head-scratcher, but the soft radishes bathed in fat are like brisket without the brisket. It just works.

The menu changes seasonally, but a few dishes stick around all year. Daily crudos are a signature, along with the craveable pea shoot salad with sesame-yogurt dressing ($13) you’ll dream about for weeks.

The housemade kimchi noodles ($20) are required. So are the Almost Famous Chicken Tenders ($18), served with housemade ranch that will take you right back to childhood, and the brisket tacos.

For dessert, the Thai iced tea shave ice with evaporated milk and whipped cream ($9) may be the best dessert you’ll have all summer.

This is a menu you’ll want to revisit: Jamaican grilled shrimp with chow chow ($17), grilled Vietnamese steak with a cube of fried sticky rice ($19), duck confit with duck-fat potatoes ($29) and the burger ($19). If you know, you know.

The drinks

Lo & Behold is all about craft cocktails, all $15, and the drink menu starts smacking its lips the moment you see it. Sangria and punches are signatures, made with seasonal fruit and spirits.

Dr. Feel Good: A mysterious combination of fruit and herbal liqueurs, allspice and seltzer — an adult Dr Pepper-ish cocktail.

K-Pop: Vodka with strawberry and melon liqueurs, lemon and yuzu. A side of tween-girl BTS tears optional.

World’s Best Vodka Soda: Locally made Young & Yonder vodka is the base, with “improved seltzer” and unicorn tears. The tears are apparently a tedious process, according to Heffernon, but worth it. It is, without a doubt, the world’s best vodka soda, primarily because of the unicorn tears — harvested by tickling unicorns until they weep with laughter.

The Caribbean Queen ($12): This spirit-free cocktail made with passion fruit, lime, orange and coconut is a Billy Ocean song in a glass. Smooth, sexy and full of soul.

The deals

Happy hour runs from 3-5 p.m. Thursday through Monday, with $9 cocktails, including sangria, ranch water, martinis and vodka sodas. The restaurant is closed Tuesday and Wednesday.

The spot

214 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-756-5021, loandbeholdca.com. Open 11:30 a.m. to midnight Thursday through Monday.

title: Newly Rebuilt Atlas Peak Winery in Napa Listed for Sale
summary:
Nestled on Napa's Atlas Peak AVA, the estate includes a three-bedroom home, fully permitted winery and 24.5-acre vineyard with valley vistas.

The post Newly Rebuilt Atlas Peak Winery in Napa Listed for Sale appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Atlas Peak, a small-production winery estate in Napa, is currently listed for sale. On a gated plateau in the Vaca Mountains, six minutes from downtown Napa, the main residence, guesthouse, barn, winery and vineyard are priced at $14,950,000.

The organic and biodynamically farmed vineyard is planted with 13 blocks of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot vines on 24.5 acres in the Atlas Peak AVA. 

The Atlas Peak appellation terroir is prized for its elevation, cool climate and volcanic soil. Founded in 1987, before the Atlas Peak region received its AVA status in 1992, the winery makes award-winning estate Cabernet. The newly built wine-making facility is permitted to produce 8,500 bottles. 

The property’s new three-bedroom, three-and-half bathroom main residence is sleek and slate-colored with contrasting spots of stone cladding. Interiors are light and airy with generous steel-framed windows and glass interior and exterior doors. On fog-free days, valley vistas extend to San Francisco’s Financial District. The property includes a pool and spa.

title: Former Salesforce CFO Lists Sonoma Estate for $12.9 Million
summary:
The Bay Area tech executive's 17-acre Sonoma home features multiple kitchens, fire pits and a bocce ball court for Wine Country entertaining.

The post Former Salesforce CFO Lists Sonoma Estate for $12.9 Million appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The Sonoma estate of Graham Smith, former chief financial officer of Salesforce, is currently listed for sale. On 17 hilltop acres with valley views and 7,370 square feet of living space, the home and guesthouse are listed for $12,900,000.

The clean-lined dwelling, with wood cladding and a series of mono-pitched roofs, was designed by Cahill Studio and built in 2015 by Landers Curry.

The home centers on a great room featuring a Hersh Design light fixture made of spun molten glass, an Ortal three-sided glass fireplace and pocket doors that provide a wide-open connection to the yard. The kitchen area has Snaidero Italian cabinetry topped with Carrara marble. A back kitchen offers space for food prep and staging. It includes a built-in coffee system, double ovens and a Grohe Blue sparkling water faucet.

The home’s three bedrooms have ensuite bathrooms. There are two powder rooms, two office spaces, a media room, game room and elevator. 

Outside, covered spaces for both lounging and dining have integrated heaters allowing year-round alfresco dining. Serving food is convenient via the adjacent outdoor kitchen. The spaces surround a substantially sized pool with a built-in spa.

Cultivar Landscape Architecture, formerly Roche + Roche, designed the landscape to blend with the rugged natural setting. The grounds include raised garden beds, a bocce ball court and three gas-start fire pits. A modern concrete fountain by Sebastopol’s Bohemian Stoneworks adds a weighty statement to a lush patch of plantings. 

Additional amenities include solar panels, an AI-enabled security system and a fire suppression system.

title: Screamin’ Mimi’s Among Washington Post’s Top US Ice Cream Shops To Build a Vacation Around
summary:
After over 30 years in business, Sonoma County locals and national publications alike are still screaming for Screamin' Mimi's in Sebastopol.

The post Screamin’ Mimi’s Among Washington Post’s Top US Ice Cream Shops To Build a Vacation Around appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Maraline Mazzetti Olson is no stranger to publicity. Her Sebastopol ice cream parlor, Screamin’ Mimi’s, has been highlighted in USA Today, Food & Wine magazine and other national outlets. But when Washington Post reporter Hannah Sampson called to tell Olson she wanted to include the shop among the top U.S. ice cream destinations to build a vacation around, the recognition felt especially personal.

Sampson told Olson that ice cream expert Malcolm Stogo had recommended Screamin’ Mimi’s for the story. Stogo is best known for inventing the popular Cookies & Cream flavor in 1978 and has consulted for major brands, including Häagen-Dazs. In 1995, he founded Ice Cream University, based in New Jersey.

Olson met Stogo more than 30 years ago.

“He has been a mentor of mine for a long time and he just has a passion for ice cream and identified the same passion in me,” Olson said. “So it’s a pretty big honor to be recommended by Malcolm Stogo.”

An ice cream passion

Olson’s passion for making ice cream grew out of longing and necessity.

In New York’s Hudson Valley, where she grew up, ice cream parlors were a fixture in every town. But after moving to Sonoma County with her husband, Kurt, 34 years ago, she noticed a lack of locally owned ice cream shops.

“There was a Baskin-Robbins, (but) there were no homemade-ice cream parlors anywhere,” she said. “I couldn’t believe that an area so focused on food didn’t care about the quality of the ice cream it was eating.”

So Olson began making ice cream at home. For years, she had been thinking about a particular flavor inspired by a coffee sundae topped with hot fudge and cookies that she tried as a kid. The dessert made her appreciate coffee ice cream — “if it had enough chocolate in it.”

That inspiration became Mimi’s Mud, the shop’s signature flavor: espresso ice cream blended with homemade fudge, chocolate chips and Oreo pieces.

“The combination was exactly what I was hoping for.”

Recognizing that she had something special, Olson and her husband opened Screamin’ Mimi’s in Sebastopol in October 1995. The shop celebrated its 30th anniversary last year.

Olson describes the business as “very mom-and-pop,” with her husband and their son Carter, a Culinary Institute of America graduate, helping run the shop.

Screaming for Mimi’s

The unassuming ice cream parlor has earned praise locally and nationally for years. It is so consistently busy that Olson has hardly noticed a change in business since The Washington Post article appeared, aside from people reaching out to congratulate her.

“This is our super busy season anyway,” she said of summer. “We are so fortunate in that we have a really healthy business as it is.”

Mimi’s Mud remains the shop’s most popular flavor, and Olson credits it with helping distinguish Screamin’ Mimi’s from other ice cream shops. In the early years, the shop once sold out of it, prompting one “particularly obsessed customer” to stand on the counter and scream at children who couldn’t have the coveted flavor.

“So I don’t ever let that happen,” Olson said. “We never run out of Mimi’s Mud.”

Other popular flavors include olive oil, lavender and Bee’s Knees, made with lavender ice cream and chocolate honeycomb. The lavender flavors are highly seasonal, available only when Olson can pick fresh lavender grown in Sebastopol.

Local love

Using local ingredients and supporting local farmers is important to Olson.

She sources peaches from Healdsburg’s Dry Creek Peach and from a former employee’s Geyserville farm. The strawberries and watermelon come from the L&N Produce Stand in Sebastopol, while raspberries are picked at Boring Farm, also in Sebastopol. More recently, she bought some “beautiful” Crane melons from Healdsburg’s Tookey Farms.

Olson’s commitment to the community extends beyond produce. For the past 27 years, Screamin’ Mimi’s has participated in Vitalant blood drives, donating a pint of ice cream for every pint of blood donated. The shop hosts one of the largest blood drives in the county, most recently held at Brook Haven Middle School in Sebastopol.

“It means a lot to me to be that active in the community,” Olson said. She and her husband also focus on supporting education and raising what she called “much-needed” funds. “We really love to support public schools … but we generally donate to anybody who asks.”

That commitment to young people and education extends to the shop’s employees, many of whom start as teenagers.

“I am super proud of the ice cream we make and the business that my husband and I and our boys have built,” she said. “But it could not be done without the amazing people who have worked for me over the years and are still currently here.”

Worth the trip

Screamin’ Mimi’s scoops 16 ice cream flavors, along with eight dairy-free options and sorbets. Vanilla, strawberry, chocolate chip cookie dough, Deep Dark Secret, Cookie Break and Galaxy are available daily. The remaining flavors change with the seasons and the availability of fresh ingredients.

Two seasonal favorites are hazelnut fudge, which Olson calls “superior to any hazelnut I’ve ever had in Italy,” and spumoni, available only in December. It combines three flavors: pistachio, chocolate with cherries and Grand Marnier with candied orange bits.

In addition to the national attention, Screamin’ Mimi’s regularly appears on Sonoma Magazine’s list of the best ice creams in Sonoma County and has frequently been named “Best Ice Cream” in The Press Democrat’s “Best of Sonoma County Readers’ Choice Awards.”

“I don’t take for granted one day that people are gonna want my ice cream over anybody else’s ice cream,” Olson said. “So I make sure that my product tastes that good that you wouldn’t want to go anywhere else.”

Screamin’ Mimi’s, 6902 Sebastopol Ave., Sebastopol, 707-823-5902, screaminmimisicecream.com

title: Meet Nicolette Hayes, Jack London State Historic Park’s Lifetime Champion
summary:
Nicolette Hayes literally grew up inside Jack London State Historic Park. Now she brings an intimate understanding of the park as a new nonprofit board member.

The post Meet Nicolette Hayes, Jack London State Historic Park’s Lifetime Champion appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
As the daughter of Jack London State Historic Park’s former resident ranger, Nicolette Hayes literally grew up inside the park. From the time she was born in 1984 until she left for college at 17, she had the run of the Beauty Ranch on Sonoma Mountain, where she played in the redwood fairy rings and had her own special wishing tree.

“It felt like the park was my own backyard,” says Hayes.

A data designer by trade, she studied geography and later Communication Design at Pratt Institute in New York. Like London, she traveled the world, but always yearned to return to Sonoma Valley. While a home in the park was no longer an option, Hayes did the next best thing, settling in Glen Ellen with her husband, Jon Schramm (a new park volunteer), and their two young children.

She brings a singularly intimate understanding of the park to her role as a new member of the board of Jack London Park Partners, a nonprofit that was created to manage the park in the wake of a state budget crisis in 2012. Her late father Greg Hayes championed the effort to keep the park open.

A favorite place

The beautiful home Jack designed for his pigs — teasingly referred to as The Pig Palace by people who thought it was a little over the top. I can’t help but admire the humaneness that is infused in every detail. From the thoughtful layout that allowed pig families to stay together with their own front yard and extensive backyard for foraging, to the joy that it brought to Jack to play with the little piglets, it feels like an example of what is possible if you allow beauty, adventure, and a little bit of love to guide decision making, which is how I’ve tried to organize my own life.

A passion project

One of the most exciting is a regenerative garden that we’re in the process of planning and building off the parking lot, which coincidentally, is one of the places where my friend and I tunneled a trail and encountered poison oak as kids. We’re going to create an actual trail that is educational and will engage kids. As a mother of small children, I’m excited to have something they can enjoy that is accessible within just a short walk.

Reflections on serving

This couple (Jack and Charmian), who sailed the world seeing the best it had to offer, still saw in Sonoma Valley “a quiet place in the country to get out of nature that something which we all need,” leading to it being preserved for future generations. The fact that Jack London Park Partners is helping to expand that appreciation to serve our community feels like such an essential service that I’m really proud to be a part of.

title: Taste Petaluma Is a New Hub for Local Wine, Food and Drinks
summary:
The new collective gathering space in Petaluma offers Barber Cellars wines, craft cocktails, cheeses and sweet treats.

The post Taste Petaluma Is a New Hub for Local Wine, Food and Drinks appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
If you were to design a tasting room that borrowed the best parts of several culinary worlds, it might look something like Taste Petaluma.

The new collective brings together Barber Cellars, the Petaluma Cheese Shop, Barber Lee Spirits, and Nightcap Dessert Bar, offering locally made wines and spirits alongside craft cocktails, cheeses, desserts and handmade chocolates.

The story

Husband-and-wife team Lorraine and Mike Barber began making wine together more than 20 years ago, when they were living in San Francisco. Mike had worked in wine retail; Lorraine’s background was in construction. In 2007, they launched Barber Cellars, initially making wine at a custom-crush facility in Suisun City.

The Barbers eventually moved into their own Sonoma County winery and began farming 10 acres of vines near Petaluma. In 2015, they opened Petaluma’s first downtown tasting room, inside Hotel Petaluma.

Mike Barber soon became interested in craft distilling. In 2017, he co-founded Barber Lee Spirits with Aaron Lee, opening a distillery in a former brick warehouse next door to the hotel. The operation began with single-malt rye, moonshine and absinthe, later adding heirloom corn bourbon, apple brandy and rum.

The couple continued expanding. They opened Petaluma Cheese Shop inside the Barber Cellars tasting room and launched Nightcap Dessert Bar at Barber Lee Spirits.

For years, the arrangement worked. But managing several businesses across two locations while farming, making wine and distilling eventually became unsustainable. The couple decided it was time to consolidate.

“The financial reality of the wine business and tourism was definitely a factor,” Mike Barber said. “The ability to have one space that melds everything we create just made sense.”

In early July, the Barbers launched Taste Petaluma as a collective space for all of their businesses inside the Barber Lee Spirits distillery.

The vibe

If you’ve visited Barber Lee Spirits for a tasting or a cocktail, the atmosphere at Taste Petaluma will feel familiar.

The space has been slightly reconfigured for the new concept, but it retains the feel of a friendly neighborhood lounge with an industrial-chic edge. The bar has moved closer to the entrance, while a cozy nook with armchairs and tables occupies the back.

Couples, friends and families mingle in the tasting room, while dogs snooze on the worn wooden floors. It is a place that invites you to settle in for a while — and you can, because Taste Petaluma stays open until 10 p.m. most days and until 11 p.m. on weekends.

On the palate

Taste Petaluma is designed for mixing and matching. There are Sonoma County wines by the glass or in flights, cocktails made with Barber Lee Spirits, artisan cheeses and locally made chocolates from Mad Chocolates.

If you’re in the mood for wine, try the Barber Cellars 2024 Sonoma Mountain Zinfandel ($45/bottle), a field blend of Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, and Alicante Bouschet with notes of berries and spice.

Cocktail lovers will get a kick out of the Treat Yo’ Self ($16), a not-too-sweet blend of Lambanog, lemon, pineapple juice, ginger liqueur and — surprise! — McEvoy Ranch jalapeño olive oil.

When you’re ready for a bite, the sharable Cheese Pull ($22) features a warm and melty wheel of Quinta cheese from Point Reyes Farmstead Cheese Co., accompanied by Della Fattoria bread and two wildly unexpected condiments: Belfare Sesame-Chili Crunch and Zinfandel chocolate sauce.

Dessert is equally playful. The Spiced Chocolate Passionfruit Cake ($16), made for Taste Petaluma by Mad Batter Cakery in Santa Rosa, layers rich chocolate cake with passion fruit filling and accents of cardamom and cayenne.

Wine tastings are $25, with wines by the glass starting at $16. Spirit flights start at $20, and seasonal cocktails are $16. Nonalcoholic cocktails, coffee and a tea service are also available.

Beyond the bottle

A few minutes’ walk from Taste Petaluma is Blanton’s Boot and Hat, a newly opened western-wear shop in a former hardware store on Petaluma Boulevard.

The boutique carries cowboy boots and hats, leather handbags and belts, turquoise jewelry and other Western-inspired goods. At the hat bar, shoppers can customize their purchases with various adornments. There are even matching cowboy hats for your pup, complete with a branded initial.

Taste Petaluma is open 3-10 p.m. Wednesday and Thursday; 3-11 p.m. Friday and Saturday; 3-9 p.m. Sunday. 120 Washington St., Petaluma, 707-971-7107, tastepetaluma.com

title: Baci Cafe & Wine Bar Reopens in Healdsburg After SUV Crash
summary:
Baci Cafe & Wine Bar has reopened in Healdsburg a little over two months after an SUV crashed 40 feet into the restaurant, causing more than $500,000 in damage.

The post Baci Cafe & Wine Bar Reopens in Healdsburg After SUV Crash appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Just over two months after an accident destroyed much of Baci Cafe & Wine Bar in Healdsburg, more than 100 people waited eagerly outside for its July 29 reopening and open house. By the end of the day, nearly 500 had come through, raising a glass to what owner Lisbeth Holmefjord has lightly called a “refresh” — one that involved more than half a million dollars in repairs.

With all-new furniture, flooring and paint, along with a new front entrance and other upgrades, Holmefjord and her husband, chef Shari Sarabi, have given the 16-year-old restaurant considerably more than a facelift. But for all the newness, Baci still looks and feels like Baci, with its familiar colors, style and charm. And it came together far faster than anyone expected.

After the Memorial Day weekend crash that sent an SUV more than 40 feet into the restaurant, the couple posted on social media that Baci would be closed until further notice. They expected repairs might take months.

The rebuilding also triggered required accessibility upgrades under current building codes, including changes to the entrance, bathrooms and back-of-house areas, adding another layer to the challenge of reopening.

Work began almost immediately, with local architects, contractors and city officials helping the longtime Healdsburg favorite get back to normal.

“It really was a community effort to get us back up and open,” Holmefjord said. “I’m so grateful for what they did and how fast it got done.”

Holmefjord has just one tiny problem: The place looks so good, and the new chairs are so comfortable, people might not want to leave.

Not a bad problem to have.

The “incident”

When Holmefjord received an early-morning call from local police about a “small incident” at the restaurant on Saturday, May 23, she wasn’t particularly worried. She and Sarabi figured they would stop by after the farmers market to investigate what sounded like a burglar alarm or a broken window.

What they found was an SUV lodged inside the restaurant.

The vehicle had taken out the front doors and windows, shredded the flooring and turned much of the dining room furniture into kindling.

“The fire chief didn’t want you to have a heart attack,” Holmefjord said of the understated warning from first responders.

Fortunately, no one was inside the restaurant at the time, and no one was injured. Police said alcohol was not a factor, and the driver was not arrested. The saving grace was that the SUV came through the restaurant’s doors and windows without striking the building’s structural supports.

“When an accident happens, it was the best outcome it could be,” Holmefjord said. “If he had hit the building, it was going to be much longer.”

The timing was particularly stressful. The collision happened over Memorial Day weekend, just as Healdsburg was heading into one of its busiest stretches of the year, with graduations, Father’s Day, weddings and large summer gatherings.

It was a blow, but Holmefjord’s first priority was keeping Baci’s 22 employees afloat during the closure.

A GoFundMe campaign organized after the crash raised about $95,000, she said, allowing the restaurant’s staff — including tipped employees — to continue receiving pay while Baci was closed.

“This way, no one got behind on their mortgage or bills,” Holmefjord said. “And they’re all happy to be back.”

For a restaurant without a dining room, the outpouring of generosity from longtime diners was touching.

Silver linings

If there’s an upside to having an SUV parked inside your restaurant, Holmefjord has found it.

“The silver lining is that the locals realized how much they missed us,” she said. “And no one was hurt.”

For Holmefjord, the past few months have reinforced how much Baci has become a local anchor in a town awash with upscale restaurants. Some customers have already returned two or three times since the reopening.

“We may not recoup everything, but we’re still gonna be here for a long time. We’re not going anywhere.”

She noted that reservations, especially in light of the reopening, are a good idea.

Baci is at 336 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg. 707-433-8111, bacicafeandwinebar.com

title: Chefs Charlie Palmer, Liza Gershman Celebrate Sonoma County Food in New Cookbooks
summary:
The new locally produced cookbooks, both with Healdsburg roots, feature chefs, farmers and artisans producing the best of Wine Country food.

The post Chefs Charlie Palmer, Liza Gershman Celebrate Sonoma County Food in New Cookbooks appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The summer bounty is officially here and with it come two new, locally produced cookbooks, both with Healdsburg roots, that celebrate the very best of local food.

James Beard Award-winning chef Charlie Palmer’s “Wineland,” penned with Healdsburg journalist Matt Villano, features 20 Wine Country culinary luminaries from Sonoma, Napa, and Marin Counties who share their life stories and favorite recipes.

“The way we live here is an ideal, a philosophy, built around hard work and relationships,” says Palmer, a Healdsburg resident who chased that dream when relocating from New York with his family 25 years ago. “We make and grow and build and create. Community is paramount — this is about the most real place you can get.”

Some of the storytelling also comes from work of local photographer Emma Kruch, who spent more than a year trekking from cloud-blanketed mountaintops to being hip-deep in brackish bay waters to capture more than 125 images that add to the book’s artistry.

Flipping through the glossy pages, you can practically taste Liam Callahan’s tangy-sweet sheep’s milk cheese dotted with herbs from Bellwether Farms in Petaluma and smell the briny air at John Finger and Terry Sawyer’s Hog Island Oyster Co. on Tomales Bay.

The Healdsburg Farmers Market is the setting for Sonoma County native Liza Gershman’s latest cookbook, “Farm + Market: Healdsburg,” which reads like a love letter to the community that revolves in and around the beloved market.

Founded in 1978, the Healdsburg Farmers Market is one of the oldest certified markets in California. Gershman, who has written and photographed 20 cookbooks, celebrates the local farmers, ranchers, makers, chefs, and even home cooks who are the heart and soul of the market that runs Saturdays, April through December, and Tuesdays, May through September. A portion of proceeds from the book goes right back into the market to ensure it continues to thrive.

Rebecca Richards is one of its champions; she fell in love with Healdsburg 15 years ago and convinced her husband they needed to move from San Francisco. After visiting the market, she quickly got swept in with the community, and before she knew it, was on the board and helping with bookkeeping.

“I’m very into recipes and going to the market to see what’s in season,” says Richards, whose recipe for an arugula, nectarine, and quinoa salad demonstrates her respect for seasonal ingredients and the farmers who nurture them. Local nectarines are at their finest in June through August.

“I think people just assume that you can get anything at any time, which you kind of can, but that doesn’t mean it’s at its peak,” she says. “It kills me when I go to a restaurant in January and they’re serving BLTs. And I’m like, ‘No!’ I have to wait for summer for a real, happy tomato.”

A Tale of Two Cookbooks

Wineland is best for:

  • Friends and family who love to visit Wine Country
  • Those who want the story behind their favorite restaurants, wineries, and producers
  • Accomplished home cooks

Find it at local bookstores and at charliepalmer.com.

Farm + Market is ideal for: 

  • Farmers Market aficionados
  • Collectors of community cookbooks
  • Local history buffs

Find it at healdsburgbook.com.

title: Bonnie Bagels Brings East Coast Classic to Sebastopol
summary:
Recently opened in the former Hippizzazz pizza space — near longtime Sebastopol favorite Grateful Bagel — Bonnie Bagels is banking on the East Coast classic.

The post Bonnie Bagels Brings East Coast Classic to Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A small Sebastopol cafe has finally cracked the code on East Coast bagels in Sonoma County.

Bonnie Bagels opened in mid-August with kettle-cooked bagels — boiled and baked, as they should be — and a line out the door.

Yes, there are other good bagels in Sonoma County. But until now, I wouldn’t have called them East Coast great. Bonnie’s aren’t just East Coast great. They’re New York great: crisp on the outside, chewy on the inside and, best of all, available in salt.

“It’s a secret hint to a certain kind of person that we’re the real deal. It’s classic East Coast,” said executive chef Greg Kalergis.

Owner Michael Sousa, who grew up near Boston, knew it was time to open a shop about 18 months ago, when the stars aligned. The former Hippizzazz Pizza space across from HopMonk was vacant. He had friends from Bageltopia in Berkeley willing to mentor the fledgling venture. And he had recently met Kalergis, now his executive chef, at a family Thanksgiving.

After more than a year of planning and construction — and plenty of flak for opening a bagel shop within spitting distance of longtime Sebastopol favorite Grateful Bagel — Sousa soldiered on.

“I understand the awkwardness of it,” Sousa said. “But the benefits of bringing this to the community outweighed that. I’m hopeful that we can provide something different enough that we can coexist in harmony.”

Besides salt bagels, the cafe offers the usual lineup of plain, sesame, poppy seed, onion and everything, along with more California-leaning flavors such as cheddar jalapeño and Asiago. Schmears include caper dill, smoked salmon, scallion, green olive and chile crisp.

There are also gluten-free bagels and vegan cream cheese, plus breakfast sandwiches and open-faced lox, tuna salad and egg salad bagels. Espresso drinks and coffee round things out.

On opening day, the shop sold out within three hours. The same thing happened the next day. After two days to regroup, the team is back with more of everything — especially those brilliantly boiled-and-baked bagels.

As for the odd, half-finished sign that currently says “Bonnie Bag”? Painting was interrupted by permitting issues. The owners expect to finish it in the next couple of weeks.

Open 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. 280 S. Main St., Sebastopol, bonniebagels.com

title: Santa Rosa’s New Capriciano Osteria Is Already Packed With Diners Eager for Italian Classics
summary:
Italian classics made with high-end local ingredients fill the tables at Capriciano Osteria, opened in Santa Rosa's former Tipsy Taco space.

The post Santa Rosa’s New Capriciano Osteria Is Already Packed With Diners Eager for Italian Classics appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County loves an Italian restaurant. Maybe it’s our broad swath of Italian immigrants; maybe it’s simply the enduring appeal of pasta and wood-fired pizza. Either way, it’s no surprise that Capriciano Osteria is already packed with eager diners a week after opening in downtown Santa Rosa.

The tables are filled with the classics — warm focaccia, burrata salad, ravioli, risotto and affogatos. The only real surprise is that the chef isn’t Italian. He’s Turkish.

Chef Baki Bekci grew up in his family’s restaurant in Fethiye, a port city and district on Turkey’s southwestern Turquoise Coast, where small fishing boats brought in the day’s catch and the menu centered on seafood and mezze. He later worked in the kitchens of Four Seasons hotels in Istanbul, Los Angeles and Calistoga before founding Mezzeluna in Cotati, which he has since left.

Now Bekci is running his own kitchen in Santa Rosa, in the former Tipsy Taco space, once home to the Acapulco Lounge. He has transformed it into a cozy dining room flanked by two large fireplaces, with an outdoor patio larger than most in the region.

The food is straightforward, built around familiar Italian-American and Italian classics, from bruschetta and Caesar salad to fresh pasta, chicken Parmesan, lamb chops and risotto. But Bekci’s fine-dining background shows in the artful plating and high-end ingredients sourced from local farms and producers.

“I just want people to feel happy and enjoy the restaurant and the food and come back again,” he said.

Best bets

Shrimp carpaccio, $22: Raw shrimp isn’t for everyone, but at Capriciano Osteria, it should be. Delicate shrimp are pounded thin and dressed with tart passion fruit vinaigrette, spicy Sicilian chile, avocado puree and croutons.

Grilled octopus, $24: Tender octopus is an oxymoron, as far as I’m concerned, but Bekci somehow gets it soft enough to cut with a spoon. It comes with a Southern Italian-style tomato-caper sauce and smashed potatoes.

Burrata salad, $19: Creamy-as-butter burrata surrounded by seasonal stone fruit, heirloom tomatoes and basil.

Ravioli al limone, $28: The lemon-cream Parmesan sauce is the real stunner here. You’ll want a piece of bread to soak up every last bit. The earthiness of the mushroom filling works beautifully with the tart citrus.

Red wine-braised short ribs, $36: A more herbal, spiced take on traditional braised beef, served with tender meat and craveable olive-oil mashed potatoes.

Risotto frutti di mare, $34: Bekci’s signature dish comes piled with shrimp, lobster and clams. It’s lemony, with a hint of basil oil.

Cherry Coffee Kick, $12: Save room for dessert. The tiramisu is composed and elegant, but the Cherry Coffee Kick — tart cherries, a hint of espresso and dark chocolate cake — really works.

Open for lunch 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Friday through Sunday. Dinner 5-9:30 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday.

505 Mendocino Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-800-7904, capriciano.com.

title: Learn the Art of Nature Journaling With Sarah Reid
summary:
Nature journaling can serve as a form of outdoor meditation as well as inspiration for environmental stewardship and conservation.

The post Learn the Art of Nature Journaling With Sarah Reid appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sarah Reid called her mustang, Oreo, her “10,000-mile horse.”

As they rode thousands of miles of Northern California trails together, the mustang taught her how to notice small details most people would simply pass by. With just a cock of his ears, the horse would point out a buck napping in the shade off in the distance or a subtle shift in the landscape. Now Reid, a naturalist and conservationist, teaches others how to slow down and observe through nature journaling workshops she leads around Sonoma County for organizations such as the Sonoma Ecology Center and Sonoma State’s Center for Environmental Inquiry.

Reid began nature journaling in 2017 while taking a California naturalist class, a requirement for the course. Though she once believed she couldn’t draw, Reid taught herself using books and online tutorials. Now, page after page of her colorful journals are filled with watercolor sketches, handwritten notes, and questions about everything from mushrooms spotted along trails to coastal wildflowers and woodpeckers flying overhead. She encourages others who feel similarly artistically uninclined to focus on meaningful engagement with what they see rather than on artistic perfection.

Workshops often begin with a simple leaf. She asks participants to trace its shape and study its texture, color, and imperfections before guiding them through the reflection process with writing prompts such as “I notice, I wonder, and it reminds me of…”

This exercise, Reid says, helps people move past the fear of not being able to draw while encouraging deeper curiosity about the natural world. “All of our nature and outdoors is so filled with things to be curious about, to wonder about and to be awed by,” she says.

During the pandemic, nature journaling served as a form of therapy for Reid that quieted all of the “external noise.” Today, the practice continues to be a meditative one, allowing her to slow down and pay “intentional attention” to the natural world around her.

Her observations have shaped the way Reid views the changing climate. Across decades spent outdoors, she has watched many species of wildflowers, which used to bloom plentifully, bloom early or not at all. She has seen how prolonged drought stresses centuries-old oak trees and how seasonal weather patterns have shifted dramatically.

Reid believes nature journaling is important, particularly as society has become increasingly disconnected from the outdoors. The act of slowing down to observe plants, animals, and landscapes, she explains, is transformative, often blossoming into environmental stewardship and conservation. “When we take and look at something with intentional curiosity and wonder and we put it down on paper, that becomes solidified in our brain,” Reid says. “This results in a sense of place and a love for the place.”

title: Hazel Restaurant Is Back in Occidental — And More Hazel Than Ever
summary:
The pot roast is braising, the vegan Caesar is back and the schnitzel hangs off the plate. Hazel has reopened in Occidental in a quirky old Victorian that may fit the beloved restaurant better than ever.

The post Hazel Restaurant Is Back in Occidental — And More Hazel Than Ever appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sometimes when a door closes, a 150-year-old yellow clapboard Victorian overlooking downtown Occidental opens.

That’s exactly what happened to Jim and Michele Wimborough of Hazel Restaurant.

This week, the couple reopened Hazel in a new home at 3688 Bohemian Highway, less than a year after closing the restaurant’s longtime location down the street. That space, at 3782 Bohemian Highway, is now home to the recently opened Bohemian Bistro.

Moving wasn’t the plan. But sometimes unexpected changes come with silver linings.

The quirky old building that once housed Barley & Hops has a historic bar filled with 19th-century charm, an airy dining room, cozy nooks for tables and just the right amount of west county character to make it feel like a neighborhood restaurant from the start.

Not surprisingly, the regulars have already begun returning, Michele Wimborough said, happy to see their favorite dishes back on the menu.

A new home

The couple spent the past eight months reworking the space, which had sat empty for several years. It wasn’t a quick turnaround, or at least not as quick as anyone would have liked. Old buildings and old equipment have a way of revealing surprises, and sometimes things simply take longer than expected. That, too, is part of being a restaurateur.

On Aug. 13, with the tables set, cookies baked, pot roast braising and sourdough starter rising, Hazel soft-opened in its new home.

Naturally, one of the fryers broke. The sourdough starter balked. That’s also part of being a restaurateur.

Otherwise, Hazel might be more Hazel than ever.

Looking out onto a redwood grove from the pale blue dining room, there’s a coziness that settles over the room. A soft banquette, old wood floors, the occasional creak and tiny decorative details that reward a closer look all fit naturally with the casual comfort food that has become Hazel’s hallmark.

The limited opening menu includes the favorites: the epic hunk of braised beef with mashed potatoes, roasted half chicken, vegan Caesar salad and the OMG Sundae with caramel and hot fudge.

The schnitzel is larger than its oversized plate, its crisp coating spilling over the edges alongside red cabbage. The Brussels sprouts with bacon may be the best you’ve ever had, with crisp leaves, tender centers and just enough caramelization.

New are flatbreads topped with Point Reyes blue cheese, caramelized onions and bacon. They’re every bit as satisfying as Hazel’s old pizzas.

It’s all there, just the same, but in a new place that feels unmistakably Hazel.

Open 5-9 p.m. Wednesday through Monday. 3688 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-6003, restauranthazel.com.

title: Westerbeke Ranch in Sonoma Doubles as a Family’s Multigenerational Homestead
summary:
A family homestead for five generations, Sonoma’s Westerbeke Ranch has hosted notable visionaries in its storied evolution from family home to retreat and conference center.

The post Westerbeke Ranch in Sonoma Doubles as a Family’s Multigenerational Homestead appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Legend has it, there are “voices” in The Valley of the Moon. The Miwok and Pomo heard them as spirits or ghosts, visible in the illusion of multiple moons, a legend retold by author Jack London in his 1913 novel of the same name. Contemporary listeners cite the voices as echoes of nature.

In either case, if voices do whisper through this valley of rolling hills, wildflowers, and scattered oaks, Sonoma’s Westerbeke Ranch would be the place to hear them. A family homestead for five generations, its wooden beams and adobe walls were drawn from the surrounding earth more than 80 years ago. In its storied evolution from family home to retreat and conference center, it has hosted notable visionaries such as Joseph Campbell, Stan Grof, Werner Erhard, and Elisabeth Kübler-Ross.

With its smooth archways, weathered beams, and ceramic-tiled roofs, the ranch feels like an authentic early Californian hacienda. Comfortable gathering spaces surround a central patio and a pool. Well-tended, but unfussy gardens wrap around pathways that lead through dappled shade to the property’s guest cabins. From furnishings and artifacts to artwork and plantings, everything has been curated to flow in harmony with the natural surroundings.

The 11-acre property on Grove Street is overseen by owner and CEO Wendy Westerbeke, who still makes her home here. She credits the rustic ambience and authenticity of the place to her grandparents, Muriel and “Dick” Van Hoosear, who purchased and built on the property in the 1930s.

Grandfather Van Hoosear, she says, was an adventurous and peripatetic builder, raised in the East Bay, who bounced between California and favorite places like Mexico, Arizona, and the Four Corners region, where he gathered inspiration, artifacts, and salvaged materials like old hardware, hinges, and tile.

The timeworn timbers of the ceiling beams, window frames, and heavy doors reveal the ridges of old-growth wood he rescued locally from aging fences and crumbling barns. “He always had a project,” Westerbeke recalls. “He would come here on weekends, jump out of his car, leave the door open, run to the tool room to do things on the property. There was a lot going on at once.”

The property’s central dining room showcases Van Hoosear’s talents. The adobe walls, now painted a warm white, were made with mud from the bottom of a former reservoir on the property. His handmade fireplace still serves as a focal point, a rustic-yet-majestic construction of local stones that occupies a charming alcove they call “the walk-in.”

A walled courtyard attached to the dining room features Spanish-style rustic brick and tilework, with arched nichos framing plants and artifacts. “This kind of patina—you can’t create this stuff,” Westerbeke says, running her hand over the deeply ridged grain of a door. “There’s so much imitation around now, but this is the real deal.”

The term “real deal” could also be applied to “Grandpa Dick” himself, who appears in black-and-white photos throughout the property, along with dozens of other historical family photos. In one, he appears with wife Muriel, wearing worn chaps and Southwestern accessories, in the Tom Mix-style cowboy chic popular in early 20th-century America.

In 1936, her grandparents put in the 40-by-70-foot pool that guests use to this day. The couple raised their three daughters there, one of whom was Westerbeke’s mother, Patricia.

In the 1960s, Patricia and her husband Donald Westerbeke began hosting yoga retreats and meditations at the ranch, riding the wave of interest in alternative healing and Eastern medicine. As word-of-mouth traveled through the psychology corridors of UC Berkeley and spiritual centers such as the Esalen Institute, a who’s-who of humanist psychologists and New Age thinkers flocked to the property for community and inspiration.

When Donald suffered a pituitary gland tumor, it was an alternative healer that suggested he explore alternative therapies. He recovered, and Westerbeke’s parents became devoted to the idea that well-being is tied to state of mind, and that changing personal attitudes can actually improve health. Westerbeke herself studied psychology specializing in art therapy and, in her 20s, returned home with a vision to help her parents grow and manage the business.

Today the property holds five charming cabins that sleep up to 48 people. With the gardens, the large dining room, and sprawling pool, it makes a popular package for weddings and family reunions.

Additionally, conference spaces offer four distinctive meeting rooms that can handle groups from 15-80 people. Westerbeke estimates 80% of her conference and retreat clientele are women—often healthcare workers, psychologists, and educators—people, she acknowledges, “who really need a break.” Others are companies seeking unity, or a fresh start. They have several repeat customers that talk about lasting bonds forged from experiences there, delightful farm-to-table meals, and memorable gatherings.

“Because it’s peaceful and has this kind of energy, remarkable things do happen here,” Westerbeke says. “I think that’s what my parents really wanted, and that’s what I want to pass down, is that this can be a respite from the world.”

On a recent weekday morning, a group of 20 or so people studying to be personal coaches sat in a circle, attention rapt on their speaker, while a colorful luncheon of fresh salads and chicken sliders awaited in the main dining room. Later they laughed and shared stories outdoors on an adjoining sunny patio overlooking the pool and grounds.

“I think one of my favorite things about this place is people’s responses to being here,” Westerbeke says. “We have guest books going back… and it’s all these people writing about how they change their lives here. They come to workshops, and they recognize something about their patterns, and they become a completely different person because of their visit here. We’re just really the vessel for this to happen in.”

Recent additions to the property include an updated residence for Westerbeke and her husband, Ted Bucklin, after the couple decided to offer the family’s main house to her daughter’s family to live in. In her new home, Westerbeke’s vivid floral paintings adorn the walls, evoking the colorful gardens of the property itself and the 163-acre Van Hoosear Wildflower Preserve across the road, which the family still owns but has set up as an open space conservation easement managed by the Sonoma Ecology Center. The lower level serves as her painting studio, complete with her own stunning landscapes, and a special area for her to “paint with the grandchildren.”

Another new addition is a tall, narrow hay-bale structure with a weathered bell and chimes that echo within its second story, creating a sound bath below. A verse from Leonard Cohen’s “Anthem” is printed on the wall:

Ring the bells that still can ring, forget your perfect offering.

There is a crack in everything. That’s how the light gets in.

The structure looks like it has been there as long as the ranch itself, a testament to the care the family puts into maintaining harmony with the property’s original design.

“A lot of our colleagues and friends are wine- and grape-oriented,” Westerbeke reflects, “And, you know, I always joke, ‘Well, we don’t grow grapes here; we grow people.’ And it’s true. You know, people come here and it’s their spirits that get touched. And it’s a different kind of nurturing, but I love that.”

Learn more about Westerbeke Ranch at thewesterbekeranch.com. Wendy Westerbeke’s art can be found at wendywesterbekeart.com.

title: Lo & Behold Bar and Kitchen Is Healdsburg’s Favorite After Work Hangout
summary:
This late-night Healdsburg spot is dark and moody, but in a cozy-nest way, not a sticky-table-and-some-guy-passed-out-at-the-bar way.

The post Lo & Behold Bar and Kitchen Is Healdsburg’s Favorite After Work Hangout appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Healdsburg has no shortage of places to drink serious wine. Lo & Behold is where you go when you’re done being serious about it and just want a good cocktail.

The downtown bar has become a magnet for locals looking for a break from “Beverly Healdsburg,” but it is a particular favorite of the hospitality industry: restaurant workers, winemakers, tasting-room staff and others finally off the clock. That is exactly what Tara Heffernon and her business partners, Sean Kelley and Laura Sanfilippo, longtime industry veterans themselves, thought the increasingly touristy town needed.

“It’s the place you’re always looking for when you’re traveling,” Heffernon said — that laid-back insider’s spot where the locals actually eat and drink. “The biggest compliment we get is that people are being sent to us from another establishment.”

Inside the cavernous dining room are comfy chairs and a sofa for lingering, high-top tables, a long banquette lined with bistro tables and plenty of seats at the bar. It’s dark and moody, but in a cozy-nest way, not a sticky-table-and-some-guy-passed-out-at-the-bar way.

Outside, the casual patio is dog- and kid-friendly, with no one fretting over a few crumbs or what you’re wearing.

Heffernon still makes the signature sangria herself, filling it with whatever fruit and herbs are in season. Right now, that means black plums and shiso. It’s an unassuming cocktail that goes down easily after a long day of wine tasting. There’s no need to discuss its legs or finish because, really, who cares? It’s just fun to drink.

Lo & Behold is also one of the few spots in Healdsburg open after 9 p.m., something Heffernon and Sanfilippo knew from experience was sorely lacking in the sleepy town.

The backstory

Heffernon and Sanfilippo were part of the founding team at Duke’s Spirited Cocktails with Cappy Sorentino and Steven Maduro in 2016. The bar became known for working backyard botanicals into its drinks, creating fresh and unusual flavors that helped fuel the craft-cocktail wave that is now almost commonplace.

The team departed in 2021. Heffernon and Sanfilippo then teamed up with chef Kelley, who had run the food program at Burdock, to open Lo & Behold.

“We had an opportunity to start our own place and we wanted to create something really special together,” Heffernon said.

Sensing something was missing from Healdsburg — a warm, friendly, casual spot with good service — they plunged into creating Lo & Behold. Nearly five years later, the place is rarely empty.

“It’s just abuzz all of the time,” Heffernon said. “We want it to feel like people are coming home.”

Fun fact

Inside the men’s room (sorry, ladies), look for the clown painting by longtime comedian Red Skelton. You’ll see it, and it may haunt your nightmares.

When Guy Fieri is filming “Tournament of Champions” or “Guy’s Grocery Games,” celebrity chefs often stop by Lo & Behold for dinner and sign the print.

How long in business

Four years — five in January, according to Heffernon. She is already sweating the grand celebration they’ll throw because, she said, it has to be epic.

Most popular dish

The Almost Famous Chicken Tenders, because they’re the kind of adult kid food that makes people feel comforted and nurtured. But the soul of the menu, Heffernon said, is the Kimchi Noodles, made with broad, housemade noodles bathed in kimchi butter and black vinegar and topped with a generous dollop of kimchi.

When it comes to cocktails, the Guava Paloma has always been at the top of the list. A juicy twist on the Mexican highball, it’s made with white tequila, guava, grapefruit, lime and lychee — a little sweet, a little sour and dangerously delicious.

The food

Chef Kelley is a chef’s chef, meaning he makes the kind of food other chefs crave. He’s not interested in culinary bravado. Instead, he puts his efforts into hearty, rib-sticking, “I’m starving, feed me” food. His creative takes on global cuisine almost always hit the mark, with bold flavors and unusual — sometimes plain wacky — combinations that just work.

Tallow-braised radishes with beef floss ($13) are a head-scratcher, but the soft radishes bathed in fat are like brisket without the brisket. It just works.

The menu changes seasonally, but a few dishes stick around all year. Daily crudos are a signature, along with the craveable pea shoot salad with sesame-yogurt dressing ($13) you’ll dream about for weeks.

The housemade kimchi noodles ($20) are required. So are the Almost Famous Chicken Tenders ($18), served with housemade ranch that will take you right back to childhood, and the brisket tacos.

For dessert, the Thai iced tea shave ice with evaporated milk and whipped cream ($9) may be the best dessert you’ll have all summer.

This is a menu you’ll want to revisit: Jamaican grilled shrimp with chow chow ($17), grilled Vietnamese steak with a cube of fried sticky rice ($19), duck confit with duck-fat potatoes ($29) and the burger ($19). If you know, you know.

The drinks

Lo & Behold is all about craft cocktails, all $15, and the drink menu starts smacking its lips the moment you see it. Sangria and punches are signatures, made with seasonal fruit and spirits.

Dr. Feel Good: A mysterious combination of fruit and herbal liqueurs, allspice and seltzer — an adult Dr Pepper-ish cocktail.

K-Pop: Vodka with strawberry and melon liqueurs, lemon and yuzu. A side of tween-girl BTS tears optional.

World’s Best Vodka Soda: Locally made Young & Yonder vodka is the base, with “improved seltzer” and unicorn tears. The tears are apparently a tedious process, according to Heffernon, but worth it. It is, without a doubt, the world’s best vodka soda, primarily because of the unicorn tears — harvested by tickling unicorns until they weep with laughter.

The Caribbean Queen ($12): This spirit-free cocktail made with passion fruit, lime, orange and coconut is a Billy Ocean song in a glass. Smooth, sexy and full of soul.

The deals

Happy hour runs from 3-5 p.m. Thursday through Monday, with $9 cocktails, including sangria, ranch water, martinis and vodka sodas. The restaurant is closed Tuesday and Wednesday.

The spot

214 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-756-5021, loandbeholdca.com. Open 11:30 a.m. to midnight Thursday through Monday.

The post Lo & Behold Bar and Kitchen Is Healdsburg’s Favorite After Work Hangout appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Newly Rebuilt Atlas Peak Winery in Napa Listed for Sale
summary:
Nestled on Napa's Atlas Peak AVA, the estate includes a three-bedroom home, fully permitted winery and 24.5-acre vineyard with valley vistas.

The post Newly Rebuilt Atlas Peak Winery in Napa Listed for Sale appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Atlas Peak, a small-production winery estate in Napa, is currently listed for sale. On a gated plateau in the Vaca Mountains, six minutes from downtown Napa, the main residence, guesthouse, barn, winery and vineyard are priced at $14,950,000.

The organic and biodynamically farmed vineyard is planted with 13 blocks of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot vines on 24.5 acres in the Atlas Peak AVA. 

The Atlas Peak appellation terroir is prized for its elevation, cool climate and volcanic soil. Founded in 1987, before the Atlas Peak region received its AVA status in 1992, the winery makes award-winning estate Cabernet. The newly built wine-making facility is permitted to produce 8,500 bottles. 

The property’s new three-bedroom, three-and-half bathroom main residence is sleek and slate-colored with contrasting spots of stone cladding. Interiors are light and airy with generous steel-framed windows and glass interior and exterior doors. On fog-free days, valley vistas extend to San Francisco’s Financial District. The property includes a pool and spa.

title: Former Salesforce CFO Lists Sonoma Estate for $12.9 Million
summary:

content:
The Sonoma estate of Graham Smith, former chief financial officer of Salesforce, is currently listed for sale. On 17 hilltop acres with valley views and 7,370 square feet of living space, the home and guesthouse are listed for $12,900,000.

The clean-lined dwelling, with wood cladding and a series of mono-pitched roofs, was designed by Cahill Studio and built in 2015 by Landers Curry.

The home centers on a great room featuring a Hersh Design light fixture made of spun molten glass, an Ortal three-sided glass fireplace and pocket doors that provide a wide-open connection to the yard. The kitchen area has Snaidero Italian cabinetry topped with Carrara marble. A back kitchen offers space for food prep and staging. It includes a built-in coffee system, double ovens and a Grohe Blue sparkling water faucet.

The home’s three bedrooms have ensuite bathrooms. There are two powder rooms, two office spaces, a media room, game room and elevator. 

Outside, covered spaces for both lounging and dining have integrated heaters allowing year-round alfresco dining. Serving food is convenient via the adjacent outdoor kitchen. The spaces surround a substantially sized pool with a built-in spa.

Cultivar Landscape Architecture, formerly Roche + Roche, designed the landscape to blend with the rugged natural setting. The grounds include raised garden beds, a bocce ball court and three gas-start fire pits. A modern concrete fountain by Sebastopol’s Bohemian Stoneworks adds a weighty statement to a lush patch of plantings. 

Additional amenities include solar panels, an AI-enabled security system and a fire suppression system.

title: Screamin’ Mimi’s Among Washington Post’s Top US Ice Cream Shops To Build a Vacation Around
summary:
After over 30 years in business, Sonoma County locals and national publications alike are still screaming for Screamin' Mimi's in Sebastopol.

The post Screamin’ Mimi’s Among Washington Post’s Top US Ice Cream Shops To Build a Vacation Around appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Maraline Mazzetti Olson is no stranger to publicity. Her Sebastopol ice cream parlor, Screamin’ Mimi’s, has been highlighted in USA Today, Food & Wine magazine and other national outlets. But when Washington Post reporter Hannah Sampson called to tell Olson she wanted to include the shop among the top U.S. ice cream destinations to build a vacation around, the recognition felt especially personal.

Sampson told Olson that ice cream expert Malcolm Stogo had recommended Screamin’ Mimi’s for the story. Stogo is best known for inventing the popular Cookies & Cream flavor in 1978 and has consulted for major brands, including Häagen-Dazs. In 1995, he founded Ice Cream University, based in New Jersey.

Olson met Stogo more than 30 years ago.

“He has been a mentor of mine for a long time and he just has a passion for ice cream and identified the same passion in me,” Olson said. “So it’s a pretty big honor to be recommended by Malcolm Stogo.”

An ice cream passion

Olson’s passion for making ice cream grew out of longing and necessity.

In New York’s Hudson Valley, where she grew up, ice cream parlors were a fixture in every town. But after moving to Sonoma County with her husband, Kurt, 34 years ago, she noticed a lack of locally owned ice cream shops.

“There was a Baskin-Robbins, (but) there were no homemade-ice cream parlors anywhere,” she said. “I couldn’t believe that an area so focused on food didn’t care about the quality of the ice cream it was eating.”

So Olson began making ice cream at home. For years, she had been thinking about a particular flavor inspired by a coffee sundae topped with hot fudge and cookies that she tried as a kid. The dessert made her appreciate coffee ice cream — “if it had enough chocolate in it.”

That inspiration became Mimi’s Mud, the shop’s signature flavor: espresso ice cream blended with homemade fudge, chocolate chips and Oreo pieces.

“The combination was exactly what I was hoping for.”

Recognizing that she had something special, Olson and her husband opened Screamin’ Mimi’s in Sebastopol in October 1995. The shop celebrated its 30th anniversary last year.

Olson describes the business as “very mom-and-pop,” with her husband and their son Carter, a Culinary Institute of America graduate, helping run the shop.

Screaming for Mimi’s

The unassuming ice cream parlor has earned praise locally and nationally for years. It is so consistently busy that Olson has hardly noticed a change in business since The Washington Post article appeared, aside from people reaching out to congratulate her.

“This is our super busy season anyway,” she said of summer. “We are so fortunate in that we have a really healthy business as it is.”

Mimi’s Mud remains the shop’s most popular flavor, and Olson credits it with helping distinguish Screamin’ Mimi’s from other ice cream shops. In the early years, the shop once sold out of it, prompting one “particularly obsessed customer” to stand on the counter and scream at children who couldn’t have the coveted flavor.

“So I don’t ever let that happen,” Olson said. “We never run out of Mimi’s Mud.”

Other popular flavors include olive oil, lavender and Bee’s Knees, made with lavender ice cream and chocolate honeycomb. The lavender flavors are highly seasonal, available only when Olson can pick fresh lavender grown in Sebastopol.

Local love

Using local ingredients and supporting local farmers is important to Olson.

She sources peaches from Healdsburg’s Dry Creek Peach and from a former employee’s Geyserville farm. The strawberries and watermelon come from the L&N Produce Stand in Sebastopol, while raspberries are picked at Boring Farm, also in Sebastopol. More recently, she bought some “beautiful” Crane melons from Healdsburg’s Tookey Farms.

Olson’s commitment to the community extends beyond produce. For the past 27 years, Screamin’ Mimi’s has participated in Vitalant blood drives, donating a pint of ice cream for every pint of blood donated. The shop hosts one of the largest blood drives in the county, most recently held at Brook Haven Middle School in Sebastopol.

“It means a lot to me to be that active in the community,” Olson said. She and her husband also focus on supporting education and raising what she called “much-needed” funds. “We really love to support public schools … but we generally donate to anybody who asks.”

That commitment to young people and education extends to the shop’s employees, many of whom start as teenagers.

“I am super proud of the ice cream we make and the business that my husband and I and our boys have built,” she said. “But it could not be done without the amazing people who have worked for me over the years and are still currently here.”

Worth the trip

Screamin’ Mimi’s scoops 16 ice cream flavors, along with eight dairy-free options and sorbets. Vanilla, strawberry, chocolate chip cookie dough, Deep Dark Secret, Cookie Break and Galaxy are available daily. The remaining flavors change with the seasons and the availability of fresh ingredients.

Two seasonal favorites are hazelnut fudge, which Olson calls “superior to any hazelnut I’ve ever had in Italy,” and spumoni, available only in December. It combines three flavors: pistachio, chocolate with cherries and Grand Marnier with candied orange bits.

In addition to the national attention, Screamin’ Mimi’s regularly appears on Sonoma Magazine’s list of the best ice creams in Sonoma County and has frequently been named “Best Ice Cream” in The Press Democrat’s “Best of Sonoma County Readers’ Choice Awards.”

“I don’t take for granted one day that people are gonna want my ice cream over anybody else’s ice cream,” Olson said. “So I make sure that my product tastes that good that you wouldn’t want to go anywhere else.”

Screamin’ Mimi’s, 6902 Sebastopol Ave., Sebastopol, 707-823-5902, screaminmimisicecream.com

title: Meet Nicolette Hayes, Jack London State Historic Park’s Lifetime Champion
summary:
Nicolette Hayes literally grew up inside Jack London State Historic Park. Now she brings an intimate understanding of the park as a new nonprofit board member.

The post Meet Nicolette Hayes, Jack London State Historic Park’s Lifetime Champion appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
As the daughter of Jack London State Historic Park’s former resident ranger, Nicolette Hayes literally grew up inside the park. From the time she was born in 1984 until she left for college at 17, she had the run of the Beauty Ranch on Sonoma Mountain, where she played in the redwood fairy rings and had her own special wishing tree.

“It felt like the park was my own backyard,” says Hayes.

A data designer by trade, she studied geography and later Communication Design at Pratt Institute in New York. Like London, she traveled the world, but always yearned to return to Sonoma Valley. While a home in the park was no longer an option, Hayes did the next best thing, settling in Glen Ellen with her husband, Jon Schramm (a new park volunteer), and their two young children.

She brings a singularly intimate understanding of the park to her role as a new member of the board of Jack London Park Partners, a nonprofit that was created to manage the park in the wake of a state budget crisis in 2012. Her late father Greg Hayes championed the effort to keep the park open.

A favorite place

The beautiful home Jack designed for his pigs — teasingly referred to as The Pig Palace by people who thought it was a little over the top. I can’t help but admire the humaneness that is infused in every detail. From the thoughtful layout that allowed pig families to stay together with their own front yard and extensive backyard for foraging, to the joy that it brought to Jack to play with the little piglets, it feels like an example of what is possible if you allow beauty, adventure, and a little bit of love to guide decision making, which is how I’ve tried to organize my own life.

A passion project

One of the most exciting is a regenerative garden that we’re in the process of planning and building off the parking lot, which coincidentally, is one of the places where my friend and I tunneled a trail and encountered poison oak as kids. We’re going to create an actual trail that is educational and will engage kids. As a mother of small children, I’m excited to have something they can enjoy that is accessible within just a short walk.

Reflections on serving

This couple (Jack and Charmian), who sailed the world seeing the best it had to offer, still saw in Sonoma Valley “a quiet place in the country to get out of nature that something which we all need,” leading to it being preserved for future generations. The fact that Jack London Park Partners is helping to expand that appreciation to serve our community feels like such an essential service that I’m really proud to be a part of.
